chapters.title: Chapter 5: Markets and the Wider Economy

lessons.title: Inflation, GDP and Interest Rates: Connecting the Macro Dots to Markets

children.text: Macro data gets reported as a stream of disconnected numbers. In practice, three of them drive almost everything that matters at work: inflation, growth and interest rates. They form a loop, and once you can see the loop you can predict roughly how markets will react to the next data release.
Nominal, Real, and the Difference That Decides Everything

markDefs.definition: The rate at which the general price level rises, measured in India mainly through the Consumer Price Index. It reduces what a given amount of money can buy.
A figure stated before adjusting for inflation. A 7% nominal return is what the statement shows, not what your purchasing power gained.
A figure after adjusting for inflation. This is the number that tells you whether you actually got wealthier.

body.caption: Close enough for everyday use. The precise version divides the growth factors, which matters only at high inflation rates.

stats.label: After 30% Tax
stats.context: Interest is taxed at your slab rate

stats.label: Real Post-Tax Return
stats.context: Purchasing power fell, even though the balance grew

body.text: A deposit that pays 7% while inflation runs at 5.5% and tax takes 30% of the interest leaves you slightly poorer than when you started. Safety and certainty are worth paying for, but it is worth knowing that you are paying.

body.title: Work Out Your Real Return
body.prompt: A fixed deposit pays 8% a year. You are in the 30% tax bracket and inflation is 6%. What is your approximate real post-tax return, in %? Use a minus sign if it is negative.
body.explanation: Post-tax return is 8% × 0.70 = 5.6%. Subtract 6% inflation and the real return is about minus 0.4%. This is why long-horizon money, such as retirement savings, is usually not left entirely in deposits, and why the tax treatment of an investment matters as much as its headline rate.

children.text: The Two Inflation Numbers, and Why They Disagree

columns.label: Consumer Price Index (CPI)
points: Measures prices households actually pay, including services
Food and beverages carry a very large weight, close to half the basket
This is the index RBI's inflation target is set against
Moves sharply with vegetable, cereal and fuel prices
Relevant to salary decisions and household budgets

columns.label: Wholesale Price Index (WPI)
points: Measures prices at the wholesale and producer level
Weighted towards manufactured goods and commodities, with no services
Not the policy target, but a useful early signal for input costs
Moves closely with global commodity and metal prices
Relevant to procurement and pricing teams

body.text: WPI and CPI often move in opposite directions for months at a time. That is not a data error. A company can be squeezed by rising wholesale input costs while consumer inflation stays tame, which is precisely the situation where margins compress and nobody in the wider economy notices.

children.text: The Loop: Growth, Inflation, Rates

body.title: How RBI Chases Inflation (Illustrative Eight Quarters)

children.text: Read the three lines together and the loop is visible.

body.title: One Full Cycle, in Six Moves

events.title: Demand Runs Hot
events.description: Growth is strong, credit is cheap, companies raise prices because customers accept them. Inflation starts climbing above target.

events.title: RBI Tightens
events.description: The MPC raises the repo rate, usually while inflation is still rising, because policy acts with a lag of several quarters.

events.title: Borrowing Gets Costlier
events.description: Loan rates reset upward, EMIs rise, projects get deferred and consumers postpone purchases funded by credit.

events.title: Growth Slows
events.description: GDP growth eases, hiring slows, discretionary demand weakens. This is the intended cost of controlling inflation.

events.title: Inflation Cools
events.description: With demand softer, price rises moderate and inflation drifts back towards target.

events.title: RBI Eases
events.description: Rates are cut, borrowing gets cheaper, and the cycle begins again. Each full loop typically takes years, not months.

body.label: What Markets Actually Trade
body.context: Markets price the expected number in advance. What moves prices is the gap between the forecast and the actual figure, which is why a good number can still trigger a sell-off if the market hoped for better.

body.title: Why Good News Sometimes Sinks the Market

children.text: Three reasons markets react in ways that look perverse:
Strong growth can mean higher rates.
A very strong growth print raises the odds that the central bank keeps rates high for longer, which lowers the value investors place on future profits. Good economic news becomes bad market news.
Expectations were already priced in.
If everyone expected inflation at 5% and it comes in at 5%, nothing happens, however dramatic the number sounds on television.
Composition matters more than the headline.
Inflation driven by one bad vegetable harvest is treated very differently from inflation spreading across services and rents, because the second kind is persistent and forces a policy response.

body.title: Read the Reaction
body.question: CPI inflation comes in at 6.8% when economists expected 5.9%. What is the most likely immediate market reaction?
options: Bond yields fall, because inflation data does not affect bonds
Bond yields rise, as markets price in tighter policy for longer
Nothing happens, since RBI meets only every two months
The rupee strengthens sharply, because high inflation attracts foreign capital
body.explanation: A big upside surprise on inflation makes rate cuts less likely and rate hikes more likely, so bond prices fall and yields rise immediately, well before any MPC meeting. Higher inflation also tends to weaken a currency over time, not strengthen it, since it erodes purchasing power relative to lower-inflation economies.

Input cost increases arriving one or two quarters later

Stronger demand, easier price increases, more competition for talent
A weaker rupee over time, and costlier imports

body.title: The Increment Letter Nobody Believes
body.scenario: You are an HR lead at a Gurugram services company finalising the annual increment budget. The average increase works out to 8%, which the leadership team considers generous. Consumer inflation has been running near 6%. During the review, an employee representative says increments have not kept pace with the cost of living, and cites rent and school fees rising faster than 6%.
body.prompt: Is the employee wrong? How would you handle the communication honestly?
body.modelAnswer: The employee is not wrong, and neither is leadership; they are measuring different things. An 8% increase against 6% inflation is a real increase of roughly 2%, so purchasing power did rise, and that is the correct framing for the budget discussion. However, CPI is an average across a basket where food and beverages carry close to half the weight, while the items dominating an urban salaried household's budget, rent, school fees, healthcare and domestic help, often rise faster than the headline index. So an employee in a metro can genuinely experience personal inflation well above 6% while the published number is accurate. Honest communication does three things. It states the real increase explicitly rather than only the nominal 8%, because employees who hear only the nominal figure feel misled once they do their own arithmetic. It acknowledges the gap between headline CPI and lived urban costs instead of arguing against people's own experience, which is an argument HR always loses. And it differentiates: a flat 8% across the board treats a high performer and an average performer identically, so the same budget spread with genuine differentiation communicates value better than an even distribution. Two practical additions worth proposing: where the company subsidises specific high-inflation costs such as transport, canteen or health cover, quantify that in the total compensation statement, since those are real and usually invisible; and if the budget cannot stretch, say so plainly and explain the constraint, rather than describing 8% as generous to people who know what their rent did this year.

body.title: Quick Check
body.textWithBlank: A return stated after adjusting for inflation is called the ___ return.
body.explanation: Nominal is what the statement shows; real is what your purchasing power gained. Any long-term financial decision should be evaluated in real terms, and after tax.

body.title: A Monthly Macro Check in Five Minutes
steps: Note the latest CPI figure and whether it came in above or below what was expected, since the surprise is what matters
Check whether the rise was driven by food and fuel or by services, because the second kind is stickier and more likely to move policy
Note the current repo rate and the MPC's stated stance, which signals direction better than the rate itself
Convert your own key business numbers from nominal to real, so growth in volumes is not confused with growth in prices
Glance at the trade deficit and crude price together, since those two largely explain rupee pressure
Before any long-term personal financial decision, calculate the post-tax real return rather than the headline rate

body.label: MOSPI: Official Statistics
body.description: The Ministry of Statistics publishes CPI, GDP and industrial production data directly, with the detailed breakdowns news coverage skips. Reading the CPI sub-group table once shows you exactly which items are driving the headline number.

points: Every macro figure has a nominal and a real version, and confusing the two misreads both business performance and personal returns
A 7% deposit with 30% tax and 5.5% inflation leaves a slightly negative real return, so safety has a measurable cost
CPI measures household prices and is RBI's target, while WPI measures producer prices and is an earlier signal for input costs
Growth, inflation and interest rates move as a loop, with policy acting on a lag of several quarters
Markets trade the surprise rather than the number, which is why strong data can trigger a sell-off
Inflation driven by services and rents worries policymakers far more than a one-off food price spike
Every macro release maps to a department: CPI to HR, WPI to procurement, rates to treasury, GDP to sales, the trade deficit to anyone paying in dollars

body.text: This lesson is for educational purposes only and does not constitute investment, tax or financial advice. All rates, inflation figures, growth numbers and data paths used are illustrative teaching examples rather than actual statistics or forecasts. Release schedules, index compositions and tax rates change over time, so verify current figures with the official source before using them in a decision.
